rows.source: UKHSA botulism prevention and public-health guidance
rows.verified: Botulism is caused by toxins produced by Clostridium botulinum and can be a serious illness.

rows.source: UKHSA botulism prevention and public-health guidance
rows.verified: Foodborne botulism can occur after eating food containing botulinum toxin.

rows.source: UKHSA botulism prevention and public-health guidance
rows.verified: Incorrectly canned, bottled, preserved or stored foods can create conditions associated with foodborne botulism.

rows.source: UKHSA botulism prevention and public-health guidance
rows.verified: Correct cooking, storage, handling and preserving practices reduce foodborne botulism risk.

rows.source: UKHSA botulism prevention and public-health guidance
rows.verified: Home preservation of herbs or garlic in oil can be difficult to control safely.

rows.source: UKHSA botulism prevention and public-health guidance
rows.verified: Wound botulism can occur when botulinum spores enter the body through contaminated injected drugs.

rows.source: UKHSA botulism prevention and public-health guidance
rows.verified: Botulism after cosmetic procedures may involve unlicensed botulinum-toxin products and can require antitoxin treatment.

rows.source: UKHSA botulism prevention and public-health guidance
rows.verified: Difficulty swallowing, slurred speech and breathing difficulty are among symptoms reported in iatrogenic botulism cases.

rows.source: UKHSA botulism prevention and public-health guidance
rows.verified: Botulism risk depends on toxin source, food or wound pathway, preparation, dose, product authenticity, exposure timing and clinical response.

rows.source: UKHSA botulism prevention and public-health guidance
rows.verified: UKHSA botulism evidence is source-, pathway-, product-, patient-, treatment- and time-specific and is not an exact parcel-level illness probability.

rows.source: UKHSA meningococcal-disease management
rows.verified: UKHSA guidance covers public-health management of individual cases and clusters of invasive meningococcal disease.

rows.source: UKHSA meningococcal-disease management
rows.verified: Public-health management includes laboratory investigation of suspected cases.

rows.source: UKHSA meningococcal-disease management
rows.verified: Guidance includes actions after a case and management of close contacts.

rows.source: UKHSA meningococcal-disease management
rows.verified: Chemoprophylaxis may be considered in healthcare or congregate settings according to the guidance.

rows.source: UKHSA meningococcal-disease management
rows.verified: Meningococcal disease can cause meningitis or septicaemia and can become life-threatening within hours.

rows.source: UKHSA meningococcal-disease management
rows.verified: Laboratory confirmation may use organism isolation from a normally sterile site or PCR detection.

rows.source: UKHSA meningococcal-disease management
rows.verified: Meningococcal infection spreads through respiratory secretions or direct close contact.

rows.source: UKHSA meningococcal-disease management
rows.verified: Vaccination programmes are an important component of prevention against specified meningococcal groups.

rows.source: UKHSA meningococcal-disease management
rows.verified: Meningococcal risk depends on serogroup, contact intensity, setting, carriage, vaccination, host factors, symptoms and response timing.

rows.source: UKHSA meningococcal-disease management
rows.verified: UKHSA meningococcal evidence is case-, contact-, serogroup-, setting-, patient- and time-specific and is not an exact parcel-level infection probability.
